subject: Medicine
summary: Mitral stenosis is a rheumatic valve disease that narrows the mitral orifice, impeding left‑ventricular filling and causing pulmonary hypertension and atrial fibrillation. It presents with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and a characteristic opening snap and mid‑diastolic rumble.

sections.p: Mitral stenosis is a fixed obstruction of the mitral valve opening, most often due to rheumatic fever. Diagnosis relies on auscultation, echocardiography, and clinical context.

t.b: Measures mitral valve area and pressure gradient; a valve area <1.5 cm² confirms stenosis and grades severity.
Shows left atrial enlargement and pulmonary vascular congestion; useful when echo unavailable.
Detects atrial fibrillation or left atrial enlargement; not diagnostic alone.

sections.p: Severity is staged by valve area and mean gradient, guiding treatment urgency.

t.b: >10 mmHg indicates severe stenosis; correlates with symptoms.

sections.p: Rheumatic fever is the leading cause worldwide, especially in low‑resource settings. Other causes include congenital stenosis and calcific degeneration in the elderly.

t.b: Genetic susceptibility to rheumatic fever; explains regional prevalence.

sections.p: Patients develop exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and cough. A loud first heart sound, opening snap, and mid‑diastolic rumble are classic auscultatory findings.

t.b: Occurs 150–200 ms after S1; indicates valve leaflet thickening.
Best heard at apex in left lateral decubitus; reflects turbulent flow.

sections.p: Echocardiography is the gold standard. When unavailable, chest X‑ray and ECG guide suspicion.

t.b: Assesses valve area, gradient, and left atrial size; confirms diagnosis.
Shows left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion; supports clinical suspicion.
Detects atrial fibrillation or left atrial enlargement; prompts anticoagulation.

sections.p: Complications include atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, hemoptysis, and systemic emboli. Red flags are sudden worsening dyspnea, hemoptysis, or new atrial fibrillation.

t.b: May indicate pulmonary edema or tamponade; urgent evaluation needed.

sections.p: Treat the underlying rheumatic process, control symptoms, and prevent complications. Definitive therapy is percutaneous balloon valvotomy or surgery.

t.b: Prevents systemic emboli in AF; warfarin is preferred in rheumatic disease.
Reduce pulmonary congestion; avoid over‑diuresis that lowers preload.
Relieves obstruction; chosen when valve area <1.5 cm² and patient is symptomatic.

sections.p: Regular echocardiographic monitoring, vaccination against streptococcal infection, and early treatment of sore throats reduce recurrence.

t.b: Tracks valve area and pulmonary pressures; guides timing of intervention.
Prevents recurrent rheumatic fever; reduces progression of stenosis.

sections.p: Mitral regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, and left ventricular failure can mimic mitral stenosis symptoms.
b: Mitral regurgitation – holosystolic murmur, not opening snap
Pulmonary hypertension – loud S2, not mid‑diastolic rumble
LV failure – S3 gallop, not opening snap

sections.p: A normal chest X‑ray can occur in early disease; a normal ECG may miss silent atrial fibrillation.
b: Early disease may show normal imaging
Silent AF can be missed on ECG

t.b: May appear normal until significant left atrial enlargement; rely on echo if suspicion high.
Paroxysmal AF may be missed; consider Holter monitoring in symptomatic patients.

faq.q: Why is the left ventricle protected in mitral stenosis?
faq.a: Because the obstruction limits preload, the left ventricle does not experience volume overload.
The valve cannot be reversed, but percutaneous balloon valvotomy or surgery can relieve obstruction and improve symptoms.

faq.q: Is anticoagulation needed in all patients?
faq.a: Only in those with atrial fibrillation or left atrial thrombus; otherwise not routinely indicated.

exam: Explain the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension in mitral stenosis.
Describe the echocardiographic criteria for grading mitral stenosis severity.
Outline the management steps for a patient with severe mitral stenosis and atrial fibrillation.
